newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian senator Colston withdraws pay rise claim.
newsitem.headline: Australian senator Colston withdraws pay rise claim.

text.p: Key Australian independent Senator Mal Colston, already under fire over allegations of excessive expense claims and other improper benefits, withdrew a request for a pay rise on Thursday.

The Labor Opposition, from which Colston defected last year, said only media publicity had caused the withdrawal of the application, which a spokesman for the Remuneration Tribunal confirmed to Reuters.
"It was only when the matter was exposed in the media this morning that Acting Senate President Colston withdrew his greedy submission," Opposition Senate Leader John Faulkner said in a statement.
The Liberal-National government had already expressed concern about the application to the tribunal, which sets the salaries of some public officials.
"If it (the claim) is not consistent with the government's wages policy, which is a three to five percent (annual) wage outcome, we're against it," Treasurer Peter Costello told reporters.
Colston last month repaid A$6,880 after a Senate inquiry found he claimed travelling allowance for travel he had not undertaken.
He blamed his office manager's sloppy bookkeeping but the government says it is considering whether to refer the matter to the police.
Colston and another independent senator are crucial to the government because it is two votes short of a majority in upper house of parliament and all other senators are strongly Left-leaning.
When he quit the Labor party, government votes delivered him the deputy presidency of the Senate and a pay rise.
He could not sit in the Senate if convicted of fraud.

Several allegations against Colston -- all of which he denies -- emerged earlier in the year and Acting Prime Minister Tim Fischer said this week that the government's inaction on the matter was damaging its image among voters'.
This was exacerbated when Colston was allowed to step up to acting president of the Senate for three weeks in the absence of the full-time president, Margaret Reid.

Faulkner said: "It is well past time that the two reports already tabled in the Senate relating to Senator Colston's travel allowance claims, be referred by the Attorney-General, Mr Williams, to the Australian Federal Police for a comprehensive investigation."
